source.title: Multiplier sequences, classes of generalized Bessel functions and open problems

accepted.question_text: Let {gamma_k}_{k>=0} be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that f(x)=sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k/k! is an entire function. For every parameter p with -p not in N, define F_p(x)=sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k/(k! Gamma(k+p+1)). Characterize exactly which such sequences {gamma_k} have the property that F_p belongs to the Laguerre-Polya class L-P of real entire functions, meaning the class of real entire functions admitting the standard Laguerre-Polya product representation with only real zeros, for every admissible p.

evidence.quote: Problem 8. Characterize all non-negative sequences {gamma_k}_0^infinity such that if f(x) = sum_{k=0}^infinity gamma_k x^k/k! is an entire function, then F_p(x) = sum_{k=0}^infinity gamma_k x^k/(k!Gamma(k + p + 1)) belongs to L - P, for -p notin N.

Definition 2. A real entire function phi(x) = sum gamma_k x^k/k! is said to belong to the Laguerre-Polya class, written phi in L - P, if it admits the representation phi(x) = c x^m e^{-a x^2 + bx} product_k (1 + x/x_k)e^{-x/x_k}.

accepted.question_text: Does the sequence {ln(k+2)/k!}_{k>=0} form a classical multiplier sequence, meaning that the diagonal operator T on real polynomials defined by T[x^k]=(ln(k+2)/k!) x^k sends every real polynomial with only real zeros to a real polynomial with only real zeros?

evidence.quote: While we believe that the sequence {ln(k + 2)/k!}_0^infinity is a multiplier sequence, we were able to establish such a claim only for an approximating sequence.

Definition 5. A sequence of real numbers {gamma_k}_0^infinity is called a classical multiplier sequence if the associated linear operator T defined by T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k has the property that for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p(x)])=0 whenever Z_C(p(x))=0.

accepted.question_text: Let {alpha_k}_{k>=0} and {beta_k}_{k>=0} be classical multiplier sequences consisting of nonnegative real numbers, where a classical multiplier sequence is a real sequence whose diagonal operator T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k preserves real-rootedness of real polynomials. Characterize all functions Psi: R x R -> R such that, for every such pair {alpha_k} and {beta_k}, the pointwise sequence {Psi(alpha_k,beta_k)}_{k>=0} is again a classical multiplier sequence.

evidence.quote: Problem 24. Let {alpha_k}_0^infinity and {beta_k}_0^infinity be multiplier sequences of non-negative real numbers. Characterize all functions Psi : R x R -> R such that {Psi(alpha_k, beta_k)}_0^infinity is again a multiplier sequence.

Definition 5. A sequence of real numbers {gamma_k}_0^infinity is called a classical multiplier sequence if the associated linear operator T defined by T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k has the property that for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p(x)])=0 whenever Z_C(p(x))=0.

accepted.question_text: Let p(x)=sum_{j=0}^n a_j x^j be a real polynomial with a_j>=0 for every j. A sequence {gamma_k}_{k>=0} is a classical multiplier sequence if T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k preserves real-rootedness of real polynomials. A sequence is a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if the same diagonal operator never increases the number of nonreal zeros of any real polynomial, counted with multiplicity. Find necessary and sufficient conditions on p(x) such that {p(k)/k!}_{k>=0} is a classical multiplier sequence, and find necessary and sufficient conditions on p(x) such that {p(k)/k!}_{k>=0} is a CZDS.

evidence.quote: Problem 36. Let p(x) := sum_{k=0}^n a_k x^k, where a_k >= 0 (k >= 0). Find conditions on p(x) such that (a) {p(k)/k!}_0^infinity is a multiplier sequence and (b) {p(k)/k!}_0^infinity is a CZDS.

Definition 4. A sequence of real numbers {gamma_k}_0^infinity is called a complex zero decreasing sequence, or CZDS, if the linear operator T defined by T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k has the property that for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p(x)]) <= Z_C(p(x)).

Definition 5. A sequence of real numbers {gamma_k}_0^infinity is called a classical multiplier sequence if the associated linear operator T defined by T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k has the property that for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p(x)])=0 whenever Z_C(p(x))=0.

accepted.question_text: Is the sequence {(1+k+k^2)/k!}_{k>=0} a complex zero decreasing sequence? Equivalently, for the diagonal operator T on real polynomials defined by T[x^k]=((1+k+k^2)/k!) x^k, is it true that T never increases the number of nonreal zeros of any real polynomial, counted with multiplicity?

evidence.quote: Problem 37. Is the sequence {(1+k+k^2)/k!}_0^infinity a CZDS?

Definition 4. A sequence of real numbers {gamma_k}_0^infinity is called a complex zero decreasing sequence, or CZDS, if the linear operator T defined by T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k has the property that for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p(x)]) <= Z_C(p(x)).

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the sequence {sqrt(k)/k!}_{k>=0} is a classical multiplier sequence and whether it is a complex zero decreasing sequence. Equivalently for the multiplier-sequence part, decide whether the real entire function phi(x)=sum_{k>=0} sqrt(k) x^k/(k! k!) belongs to L-P+, the nonnegative-coefficient part of the Laguerre-Polya class. Here a classical multiplier sequence is one whose diagonal operator T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k preserves real-rootedness of real polynomials, and a CZDS is one whose diagonal operator never increases the number of nonreal zeros of any real polynomial.

evidence.quote: We conjecture that the function phi(x) = sum_{k=0}^infinity sqrt(k) x^k/(k!k!) belongs to L - P+.
It is not known whether phi(x) = sum_{k=0}^infinity sqrt(k) x^k/(k!k!) belongs to L - P+.
Problem 39. Determine whether the sequence {sqrt(k)/k!} is (a) a multiplier sequence (b) a CZDS.

accepted.question_text: For every real number s>0, does there exist an integer m>=1 such that the entire function sum_{k>=0} k^s x^k/(k!)^m belongs to L-P+? Here L-P+ denotes the subclass of the Laguerre-Polya class consisting of real entire functions whose Taylor coefficients are all nonnegative.

evidence.quote: Problem 40. Is it true that for every s in R^+, there exists an m in N, such that sum_{k=0}^infinity k^s x^k/(k!)^m belongs to L - P+.
If gamma_k >= 0 for k = 0, 1, 2, ..., we write phi in L - P+.

accepted.question_text: Let gamma_k=1/(k+1)^(k+1) for k>=0. Determine whether the sequence {gamma_k/k!}_{k>=0}={1/((k+1)^(k+1) k!)}_{k>=0} is a classical multiplier sequence, and determine whether it is a complex zero decreasing sequence. A classical multiplier sequence preserves real-rootedness under the diagonal operator T[x^k]=gamma_k x^k; a CZDS is a sequence whose diagonal operator does not increase the number of nonreal zeros of any real polynomial.

evidence.quote: Problem 43. Let gamma_k := 1/(k + 1)^(k+1), k in N_0. Determine whether the sequence {gamma_k/k!}_0^infinity is (a) a multiplier sequence (b) a CZDS.
We conclude this paper with one more open problem that (i) may be useful in the study of CZDS and (ii) is related to our results in Section 4.

accepted.question_text: Characterize all classical multiplier sequences {gamma_k}_{k>=0} that admit a C_k-representation. This means that there exist not-necessarily-distinct functions phi and Phi in L-P+ and real parameters s,t such that gamma_k=C_k^{phi,Phi}(t,s) for every k>=0, where B_k^phi(t)=sum_{j=0}^k binom(k,j)(1-t)^j gamma_{k-j} t^{k-j} when phi(x)=sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k/k!, and C_k^{phi,Phi}(t,s)=sum_{j=0}^k binom(k,j) B_j^phi(t) B_{k-j}^Phi(s). Here L-P+ is the nonnegative-coefficient part of the Laguerre-Polya class, and a classical multiplier sequence is a real sequence whose diagonal operator preserves real-rootedness of real polynomials.

evidence.quote: Definition 31. Let gamma_k in R for k = 0, 1, 2, .... We say that the sequence {gamma_k}_0^infinity has a C_k-representation, if there exist functions phi, Phi in L - P+ (not necessarily distinct) and s, t in R such that gamma_k = C_k^{phi,Phi}(t, s) for all k in N_0, where C_k^{phi,Phi}(t, s) is as defined in equation (4.2).
C_k^{phi,Phi}(t, s) := sum_{j=0}^k binom(k,j) B_j^phi(t) B_{k-j}^Phi(s).
B_k^phi(t) = sum_{j=0}^k binom(k,j)(1 - t)^j gamma_{k-j} t^{k-j}.
Problem 44. Characterize all multiplier sequences which have a C_k-representation.

accepted.question_text: Let beta_k=e^{sqrt(k)}/k! for k>=0, and for each n>=0 let the nth Jensen polynomial associated with {beta_k} be g_n(x)=sum_{k=0}^n binom(n,k) beta_k x^k. The source reports that g_n has only real zeros for every 1<=n<=30. Does g_n have only real zeros for every n>=1?

evidence.quote: Definition 7. Let T = {gamma_k}_0^infinity be a sequence of real numbers. For n in N_0, we define the nth Jensen polynomial associated with the sequence T to be g_n(x) := T[(1+x)^n] = sum_{k=0}^n binom(n,k) gamma_k x^k.

Let beta_k := e^{sqrt(k)}/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, .... On the other hand, our numerical work shows that the Jensen polynomials of degree n (1 <= n <= 30), associated with the sequence {beta_k}_0^infinity, have only real zeros.
